source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lou (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: The model writes a hypothesis plus a debugger command, the command is really run, the model reads the output and concludes supported, rejected or undecided. The loop repeats, then a fix is made. Repair quality stays about the same as plain prompting.
numbers: ARHE (HumanEval with one-line mutations): correct patches 177 vs 187 for the two LLM arms (table columns are garbled in the text, so which is which is uncertain). Defects4J v1.2: 76 correct for AutoSD vs 87 plain LLM. Defects4J v2.0: 113 vs 110.
limits: Not a clear gain over plain prompting; the aim was explanation. Mutation bugs in small functions. Codex and ChatGPT era models.
agent_relevance: A hypothesis-experiment-conclusion loop costs no accuracy and gives a readable trace. Do not expect a repair gain from the format alone.

source: Kang et al. (2023) AutoSD, RQ2 debugger ablation and DONE token
finding: When real debugger output is replaced by output the model imagines, results get worse. A self-declared done token only predicts quality when real execution feeds it.
numbers: Individual runs plausible: 73% with real execution vs 63% with hallucinated debugger. DONE predicted: 12.4 points more likely plausible with real execution, 11 points LESS likely with hallucinated output. With DONE and a plausible patch, 89% correct; without DONE, 82%.
limits: Small ablation; ARHE benchmark only.
agent_relevance: Supports G2 and G3: a hypothesis test must be real output from code, never a simulated one. A stop signal from the model is trustworthy only after real runs.

source: Kang et al. (2023) AutoSD, RQ4 human study of hypothesis explanations
finding: Showing the hypothesis trail beside a patch did not change review time. It raised judgement accuracy on 5 of 6 real bugs. On one bug plausible but wrong reasoning misled reviewers.
numbers: 20 participants (14 students, 6 professionals), 12 review problems. More accurate with explanation in 7 of 12 cases, worse in 2 (ARHE105, BIP003). 70% said explanations matter for repair tools; 55% liked the scientific-debugging detail.
limits: Small sample, no significance on time.
agent_relevance: A hypothesis log can mislead a reader when the reasoning is fluent but wrong. Keep the program, not the log, as the judge.

source: Straubinger, Kreis, Lukasczyk, Fraser (2025) Mutation Testing via Iterative LLM-Driven Scientific Debugging
finding: Scientific-debugging prompts (hypothesis, experiment, conclusion) were used to write tests that kill mutants. They matched a plain iterative-refinement arm and beat the search tool Pynguin on mutation score, but cost more than the plain iterative arm.
numbers: gpt-4o-mini, up to 1,000 sampled mutants per project. Branch coverage about 80% for iterative and both scientific arms vs about 55% for single-shot baseline. Line coverage about 90% vs 75%. Total cost: baseline 5.09 USD, iterative 37.1, scientific 0-shot 52.4, 1-shot 58.6 (about 41% more than iterative). Pynguin 30-run total about 12.5 USD.
quote: This result is surprising, as the scientific approaches aim to generate tests iteratively based on hypotheses
limits: One small model, test generation not debugging. Authors flag coverage as an indirect measure.
agent_relevance: At equal outcome the hypothesis format cost about 41% more tokens. Under G7 it has not paid for itself here.

source: Samir and Rahman (2026) Improved Bug Localization with AI Agents Leveraging Hypothesis and Dynamic Cognition (CogniGent)
finding: A multi-agent bug locator generates hypotheses, walks the call graph to test them, and an independent observer agent scores the evidence against the hypotheses. It beats six baselines.
numbers: 591 bug reports. MAP gain 23.33-38.57% (document and method level), MRR gain 25.14-53.74% over baselines. Ablation (Devstral), document-level MAP: removing investigation 0.360 (-11.57%), filtering 0.364, hypothesis generation 0.379, restructuring 0.382, observer 0.392 (-3.69%). Method level: investigation -19.02%, filtering -16.37%, hypothesis -13.71%.
limits: Ablation removes a whole module, not the hypothesis wording. Baselines have different designs. Cost is more than double some baselines.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis generation helps, but evidence investigation helps more. The observer scores fit of evidence to each hypothesis, in line with G5.

source: Xiong (2026) Hypothesis generation and updating in large language models
finding: In the number game, models are near Bayesian but over-favour narrow hypotheses. Models pick more correct hypotheses when asked to evaluate a list than when asked to generate their own, and generated ones are simpler and more rule-like. Behaviour on unseen parts of the domain is poor.
numbers: Three probes (posterior prediction, hypothesis evaluation, hypothesis generation) over many open and closed models. Thinking mode or telling the model the examples are incidental reduces the narrow bias. Trained only on 1..100 and queried to 200, models generalise poorly.
limits: Toy domain, not code. Numbers are mostly in figures.
agent_relevance: Generation and evaluation give different posteriors, so generate a hypothesis list and score it with code, not by asking the generator.

source: Hu, Kuang, Sun, Yang, Wu (2024) Leveraging Print Debugging to Improve Code Generation in LLMs
finding: Having the model insert print statements and read the log beats rubber-duck line-by-line explanation on easy and medium problems. Nothing helped on hard ones.
numbers: GPT-4, Leetcode. Print debugging beats rubber duck by 1.5 points (easy) and 17.9 points (medium). Plain GPT-4 about 76% easy, 26% medium, 7% hard. Hard level about 5% for all methods.
limits: Preprint, one model, self-collected Leetcode set that may overlap training data.
agent_relevance: Observation from real runs beats reasoning about code in the head. Supports probe operators with real output.

source: Chen, Lin, Scharli, Zhou (2023) Teaching LLMs to Self-Debug
finding: Models explain their code line by line (rubber duck) and read test output, then fix. Gains are largest when unit tests give real feedback.
numbers: Spider text-to-SQL, no tests: +2-3% with explanation, +9% on hardest level. TransCoder and MBPP with unit tests: up to +12%. Explanation alone on code translation +2-3%.
limits: Older models (Codex, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 era). Gains are small when tests are absent.
agent_relevance: Execution feedback carries the gain; explanation adds a little. Rubber duck alone is a weak form of hypothesis testing.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: Self-repair gains are small once cost is counted. The limit is the model's own diagnosis (its feedback). A stronger model's or a human's diagnosis lifts repair a lot.
numbers: Replacing GPT-4's own explanation with a human's raised repaired-pass fraction from 33.3% to 52.6% (1.58x). By difficulty GPT-4 feedback 42.64% intro, 19.33% interview, 3.67% competition; human feedback 62.21%, 45.67%, 14.67%. 16 participants.
limits: Small human study; HumanEval and APPS; 2023 models.
agent_relevance: The quality of the hypothesis about why code fails is the bottleneck, not the patch step. This echoes the six-fold human gain from supplied hypotheses and points to a hypothesis-breadth operator.

source: Levin, van Kempen, Berger, Freund (2025) ChatDBG
finding: An agent given debugger control (stack, variables, why-questions) finds root causes. A follow-up turn adds a lot even with no new information.
numbers: Python programs: plain why prompt 57% actionable fix, targeted question 67%, one follow-up 85%. C/C++ crashes: root cause fixed 36%, proximate cause fixed another 55%. Under 0.20 USD per fix. Over 75,000 downloads.
limits: Authors wrote the criteria; the follow-up text was identical, so extra gain may come from a second sample, not new reasoning.
agent_relevance: The 67% to 85% jump from a content-free follow-up is a second-attempt effect. Compare with plain resampling at equal tokens before crediting hypotheses.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym: A Text-Based Environment for Interactive Debugging
finding: Giving agents a Python debugger helps strong models but can hurt weak ones. Handing the debugger over only after five failed rewrites beat using it from the start or never.
numbers: SWE-bench-Lite, three runs. Claude 3.7 Sonnet: rewrite-only 37.2%, debugger from start 48.4%, debugger after 5th rewrite 52.1%. Llama-3.3-70B: 2.4 / 4.0 / 4.8%. For GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama the debugger from the start could to some extent harm results; debug(5) beat rewrite-only in all cases. Columns for other models are garbled in the text.
limits: Minimal agent design, no debugger training; authors say weak models do not know how to use pdb.
agent_relevance: A signal-gated switch (change method only after failures) fits G1. Probing tools are a skill; do not give them to a weak model unconditionally.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym, Aider and Mini-nightmare results
finding: On simple code-generation tasks (Aider) the debugger added little. On ten tricky buggy scripts (Mini-nightmare) agents with pdb often did better. Weak models kept rewriting the wrong chunk and missed a range error that stronger models named at once.
numbers: Aider: rewrites help but with diminishing returns. Mini-nightmare: the patcher task had zero success for weaker models.
limits: Ten tasks only.
agent_relevance: Failure here looks like fixation: repeat the same rewrite on the same region. A repeat detector in code could trigger a new hypothesis.

source: Debugging Decay Index paper (2025) The Debugging Decay Index: Rethinking Debugging Strategies for Code LLMs
finding: Iterative debugging effectiveness decays exponentially. Most models lose most of their repair power within 2-3 attempts. Clearing the history and restarting at computed points helps.
numbers: Abstract: most models lose 60-80% of debugging capability within 2-3 attempts. Fresh start at DDI points: llama3.1:8b 72.56% to 82.82%; deepseek-coder-v2:16b 84.1% to 92.1%; Mistral 54.3% to 62.8% and 57.3%. All six models improved. phi4-reasoning started lower but gained 21.95 points vs 9.75 for phi4.
limits: HumanEval is saturated and contamination-prone; local small models; fit quality varies by model.
agent_relevance: A machine form of fixation: the context of failed attempts anchors the next one. A code-triggered restart of context supports the reframe operator, gated on a decay signal (G1).

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Eleven LLMs show confirmation bias in a Wason rule-discovery game: they test examples that fit their guess instead of ones that would break it. More disconfirming tests go with more success.
numbers: Human baseline quoted: 29 participants, 21 found the rule; first-guess-correct people had incompatible:compatible test ratio 1.79 vs 0.24. Earlier LLM benchmark best 26%. Interventions raised mean rule discovery from 42% to 56%. Think-in-Opposites improved success in all model settings, Dual-Goal in 8 of 11. Example Qwen3-32B thinking I:C 0.14 baseline, 0.54 Think-in-Opposites, 0.77 Dual-Goal.
limits: Gains significant for thinking models only; for non-thinking models mixed. Synthetic rules.
agent_relevance: A prompt asking for a test that would prove the current hypothesis wrong works on reasoning models. It still needs a real oracle (code), not the model's judgement.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify, distillation and Blicket transfer
finding: Training the intervention behaviour into small models raised success and transferred to a new hypothesis-testing task (Blicket test).
numbers: Qwen3-8B baseline thinking success 0.21; distilled versions reach up to 0.44 with cross-scale distillation (table text partly garbled).
limits: Training is outside our no-training rule; useful only as evidence of what matters.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the falsification habit, not extra tokens alone, changes results.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench
finding: Twelve LLMs play a hidden-rule game with semantic rules. Reasoning models are better, and the main driver of success is negative testing. Confirmation bias, not oracle noise, predicts failure.
numbers: Best instruction-tuned model DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, others 33-35%. Reasoning: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%. Smallest reasoning models weak: GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%. Share of positive tests: reasoning models 24-39%, instruction-tuned 66-82%. Confirmation bias strong negative predictor (posterior mean -4.15, OR 0.016); oracle error no credible effect. n=1,200 games.
limits: Positive tests can be right when the hypothesis is narrower than the rule; authors annotate this with an LLM annotator.
agent_relevance: Count the share of probes aimed to break the leading hypothesis. This is computable in code and gateable.

source: Chari and Pattanaik (2026) Wild Guesses and Mild Guesses in Active Concept Learning
finding: In a Bayesian learner whose hypotheses are programs written by an LLM, the information-optimal query policy fails on simple concepts because it pushes the posterior where the LLM writes invalid or overly specific programs. The positive-test strategy keeps proposals valid and converges faster on simple rules.
numbers: Number Game tasks; EIG wins when falsification is needed (compound or exception-laden rules), loses on simple concepts. No single headline number.
limits: Under review, number game only, particle approximation.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation: confirming tests can be rational when the hypothesis generator is weak. Use falsifying probes when a check has failed (G1).

source: Ni et al. (2024) NExT: Teaching LLMs to Reason about Code Execution
finding: Training with execution traces of variable states and chain-of-thought explanations of runtime behaviour raises program repair. Removing traces at test time costs only a little after training.
numbers: PaLM 2: fix rate +26.1% absolute on MBPP-R, +14.3% on HumanEval-Fix-Plus. Without traces at test time 40.8% on MBPP-R, 21.8% above 3-shot baseline, 3.3% below the trace-trained run. Prompting with traces alone: average drop of 7.8% versus vanilla prompting for some models.
limits: Needs training; the prompt-only route showed weak or negative gains.
agent_relevance: Putting a trace in the prompt without training did not reliably help, so the scaffold must also say how to turn a trace into a hypothesis.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: Human baseline for this angle: supplied hypotheses made 20 developers about six times as likely to fix; supplied locations did not help.
numbers: From SUBFIELDS.md summary, not reread here.
limits: Not opened in this angle; other angles cover it.
agent_relevance: Olausson 2024 (human vs model feedback, 1.58x) is the closest LLM analogue.

source: Zeller (2002/2009) Isolating cause-effect chains / Why Programs Fail
finding: Source of the explicit hypothesis, prediction, experiment, conclusion loop that AutoSD and Straubinger copy; delta debugging as automated hypothesis testing.
limits: Recalled from knowledge; not opened.
agent_relevance: Older computational ancestor of the hypothesis loop in agents.

source: Shapiro (1983) Algorithmic Program Debugging
finding: Early AI debugger that asks an oracle about subcomputations and narrows to the faulty clause by divide and conquer. A recent LLM descendant exists (arXiv 2603.20334, ARC-AGI-2), seen only in a title listing.
limits: Recalled; not opened.
agent_relevance: Binary narrowing with a real oracle is code-checkable.

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline
finding: Why and why-not questions over a recorded execution as a way to navigate causes; ancestor of ChatDBG-style why-is-x-null questions.
limits: Recalled; not opened.
agent_relevance: Questions anchored to observed output reduce free guessing.

source: Banatt et al. (2024) Wason 2-4-6 as an LLM multi-turn benchmark (as cited in Jhaveri et al. 2026)
finding: Earlier LLM adaptation of the 2-4-6 task: up to 30 test triples then a guess; best model 26% (N=50). Read only via the citing paper.
numbers: best 26%, N=50 (via Jhaveri et al.)
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Shows how weak earlier models were at hypothesis exploration.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Practice, as cited in SUBFIELDS.md
finding: Human comparator: professionals mostly held vague speculation, not formal hypotheses, so a forced written prediction may not match what works for humans.
numbers: 7 professionals, 17 tasks; from SUBFIELDS.md.
limits: Not opened here.
agent_relevance: Formal hypothesis loops in LLMs are a design choice, not a copy of human practice.

source: Gap statement for this run: no LLM replay of Alaboudi-LaToza supplied-hypothesis conditions found
finding: Within the search quota no study was found that gives a model supplied correct, wrong or no hypotheses and measures repair as in the human experiment. Closest are Olausson 2024 and AutoSD.
limits: WebSearch quota ran out mid-task; later queries were arXiv title searches only, so absence is not proven.
agent_relevance: Open test for us: supply k generated hypotheses, test each by code, compare at equal tokens.
